learn.hook: Which sweet does your class love most? Don't guess. Collect the data and find out!
points: Data is a collection of facts, like numbers or names, gathered to answer a question.
Tally marks help us count as we collect: draw one stroke for each item, and make the fifth stroke cross the first four to make a bundle of 5.
A frequency table lists each item and how many times it appears (its frequency).
Arranging data in order, from smallest to largest, makes it easy to find the biggest and smallest values.
Check your total: the frequencies should add up to the number of things you counted.

example.q: Arjun asked 15 friends their favourite fruit: mango 7, banana 3, apple 5. Make tally marks and find the favourite.
steps: Mango: one bundle of 5 and 2 strokes = 7
example.answer: Mango is the favourite, chosen by 7 friends.

learn.reallife: Shopkeepers count which items sell most before Diwali, and cricket scorers keep data on every ball bowled.

games.title: Match the tally to the number
Data detectives
items: In tally marks, the fifth stroke is drawn across the first four.
This makes bundles of 5 that are easy to count.
A frequency table shows how many times each item appears.
Data can only be numbers, never words like 'mango'.
Names, colours and choices are data too.
A bundle of 5 and 2 more strokes stand for 7.
Sorting data from smallest to largest makes it harder to find the biggest value.
After sorting, the biggest value is simply at the end.

quiz.q: A tally shows 3 bundles of five and 2 single strokes. What number is this?
quiz.explain: Each bundle is 5, so 3 bundles make 15, and 2 more strokes make 17.
quiz.mistake: Writes the 3 and the 2 side by side (32) or forgets the single strokes

quiz.q: Meena asked her class how they come to school: Bus 12, Walk 8, Cycle 5, Car 3. How many children did she ask?
quiz.explain: Add all the frequencies: 12 + 8 + 5 + 3 = 28.
quiz.mistake: Forgets one group, or counts the number of groups (4)

quiz.q: Using Meena's data (Bus 12, Walk 8, Cycle 5, Car 3), how many more children come by bus than by cycle?
quiz.explain: 'How many more' means subtract: 12 − 5 = 7.
steps: So 7 more children come by bus.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two numbers (17) instead of finding the difference

quiz.q: How do you show 14 using tally marks?
quiz.explain: 14 = 5 + 5 + 4, so it is 2 bundles of five and 4 single strokes.
steps: Answer: 2 bundles of five and 4 strokes
quiz.mistake: Reads the digits 1 and 4 as 1 bundle and 4 strokes (which is only 9)

quiz.q: Scores in 6 cricket matches: 45, 12, 67, 30, 89, 54. Arrange them from smallest to largest. Which score is third?
quiz.explain: In order: 12, 30, 45, 54, 67, 89. The third score is 45.
quiz.mistake: Picks the third score from the unsorted list (67)

quiz.q: At a Makar Sankranti fair, Kabir counts 20 kites: red 6, yellow 4, green 3 and the rest blue. How many kites are blue?
quiz.explain: Red, yellow and green make 6 + 4 + 3 = 13. The rest: 20 − 13 = 7 blue kites.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total of the other colours (13) instead of what is left

quiz.q: What is the best way to find out the favourite sweet of the students in your class?
options: Ask every student and record the answers with tally marks
Count the sweets in a shop
quiz.explain: To answer a question about the class, collect data from everyone in the class and record it carefully.
steps: The question is about the whole class.
So collect data from every student, not from a guess or one friend.
Record the answers with tally marks so they are easy to count.
Answer: Ask every student and record the answers with tally marks
quiz.mistake: Thinks one person's choice tells us about the whole class

quiz.q: In a frequency table of favourite colours, what does 'frequency' mean?
options: How many times each colour was chosen
The largest number in the table
The name of the person who chose it
quiz.explain: Frequency tells us how many times something appears in the data.
steps: A frequency table lists each colour and a number next to it.
That number tells how many times the colour was chosen.
So frequency = how many times each colour was chosen.
Answer: How many times each colour was chosen
quiz.mistake: Confuses the item with how often it appears

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know which fruit all the birds like most: 'How do I collect and count everyone's answer?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Ask everyone, tally as I go, then make a table. Now I know it's guava!
teach.nudge: Once I have everyone's answers, how do I keep count without getting muddled?

revise.summary: Data is a collection of facts gathered to answer a question. Tally marks help us count as we collect, and a frequency table lists each item with how many times it appears.
focus: Read and draw tally marks in bundles of 5
Make a frequency table and check that the frequencies add up to the total
Arrange data in order to find the biggest and smallest values
Find totals by adding and differences by subtracting
remember: Tally: one stroke per item; the fifth stroke crosses the first four to make a bundle of 5
Frequency: how many times an item appears
The frequencies should add up to the number of things counted
traps: 3 bundles and 2 strokes is 17, not 32
14 in tally is 2 bundles of five and 4 strokes, not 1 bundle and 4 strokes
Sort the data before picking the third value

learn.hook: Should the school picnic go to the zoo or the planetarium? Don't guess. Ask!
points: Some questions can be answered without collecting data: 'How many days are in a week?' Others need data: 'Which game does our class like most?'
A survey collects answers from a group of people. Plan it first: what question will you ask, whom will you ask and how will you record answers?
Ask a clear question with fixed choices, for example 'Which is your favourite: cricket, kho-kho, football or badminton?'
Record answers with tally marks, make a frequency table, then write what you found: the most and least popular, and how many in all.
A conclusion must come from the data, not from what you hoped: 'Most of our class (14 of 30) chose cricket.'

example.q: Plan a survey to find the most popular snack in your class.
steps: Question: 'Which snack do you like most: samosa, idli, poha or fruit?'
Ask every classmate once and mark a tally for each answer.
Count the tallies, make a frequency table and find the snack with the highest frequency.
example.answer: Ask everyone, tally, make a table, conclude

learn.reallife: Election exit polls, the census and a school canteen deciding its menu all collect data through surveys.

games.title: Need to collect data?
items: How many students walk to school
Most popular TV show in our street
How many sides a hexagon has
Shoe sizes of our cricket team
Number of letters in the word INDIA

games.title: Survey steps
items: Ask and record with tally marks

quiz.q: Which question needs data to be collected?
options: Which fruit do most students in our class like?
How many months are in a year?
How many sides does a square have?
quiz.explain: Only the favourite fruit depends on what people say, so we must ask them.
steps: Facts like months in a year, 12 × 12 and sides of a square have fixed answers.
The favourite fruit depends on what each student says.
So we must ask the students and collect data.
Answer: Which fruit do most students in our class like?
quiz.mistake: Thinks every question needs a survey

quiz.q: Ravi wants the favourite game of his class of 30. Whom should he ask?
quiz.explain: To know about the whole class, he should ask everyone in it.
steps: Ravi wants to know about the whole class of 30.
So he must ask everyone in the class.
Asking only a friend, only boys or the teacher would miss others.
quiz.mistake: Asks too few people

quiz.q: Which survey question is the clearest?
options: 'Which do you like most: mango, banana, apple or guava?'
quiz.explain: A clear question with fixed choices is easy to answer and record.
steps: A clear survey question is easy to answer and record.
'Which do you like most: mango, banana, apple or guava?' gives fixed choices.
So the third question is the clearest.
Answer: 'Which do you like most: mango, banana, apple or guava?'
quiz.mistake: Asks a vague question

quiz.q: In a survey of 32 students, 14 chose cricket, 8 football, 6 kho-kho and the rest badminton. How many chose badminton?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract from the total

quiz.q: From that survey (cricket 14, football 8, kho-kho 6, badminton 4), which conclusion is correct?
options: Cricket was the most popular, chosen by 14 of 32
quiz.explain: Cricket has the highest frequency, 14 of 32.
steps: The highest frequency is 14, for cricket.
Football was not chosen by most; some did choose kho-kho; not everybody chose badminton.
So: cricket was most popular, chosen by 14 of 32.
Answer: Cricket was the most popular, chosen by 14 of 32
quiz.mistake: Draws a conclusion not supported by the data

quiz.q: Tara surveyed 25 people about their favourite festival. Her tally total is 27. What should she do?
options: Check her tallies, because she may have counted someone twice
quiz.explain: Frequencies should add to the number of people asked. 27 ≠ 25 means a mistake.
steps: Frequencies must add up to the number of people asked.
She asked 25 people but the tally total is 27.
27 ≠ 25, so she probably counted someone twice.
Answer: Check her tallies, because she may have counted someone twice
quiz.mistake: Ignores the total check

quiz.q: In the cricket survey, how many more students chose cricket than kho-kho?
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Why is it better to record survey answers with tally marks while asking?
options: They make counting quick and in bundles of 5
quiz.explain: Tally bundles of 5 make it easy to count the total at the end.
steps: Tally marks are made while asking, one mark per answer.
Every fifth mark crosses the four before it, making bundles of 5.
Bundles of 5 are quick to count at the end.
Answer: They make counting quick and in bundles of 5
quiz.mistake: Thinks tally marks are just decoration

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know the favourite worm of all baby birds. 'Should I just guess?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Ask everyone, tally the answers, and count. Data beats guessing!
teach.nudge: How will you find out what the other birds like?

revise.summary: Some questions need data; a survey collects answers from a group of people. Plan the question, whom to ask and how to record, then tally, make a frequency table and draw a conclusion from the data.
focus: Tell which questions need data to be collected
Write a clear survey question with fixed choices
Check the tally total against the number of people asked
Write a conclusion that the data supports
remember: Plan a survey: what question, whom to ask, how to record
Steps: ask everyone, tally, make a table, conclude
A conclusion must come from the data, not from what you hoped
traps: Not every question needs a survey: 'How many days are in a week?' does not
Don't ask too few people; ask the whole group you want to know about
If the tally total doesn't match the number asked, check for someone counted twice

learn.hook: A picture is worth a thousand numbers! Graphs let you see data at a glance.
points: A pictograph shows data with pictures. A key tells what one picture stands for, like 1 🥭 = 4 mangoes.
Half a picture stands for half the key value.
A bar graph uses bars of the same width with equal gaps. The length of each bar shows the value.
A scale such as 1 unit = 10 children lets big numbers fit on the page. Choose a scale that keeps bars a sensible size.
Every graph needs a title and labels on both axes so readers know what it shows.

example.q: Key: 1 🥭 = 4 mangoes. A row shows 5 whole 🥭 and half a 🥭. How many mangoes?

learn.reallife: Newspapers show cricket run rates and rainfall with bar graphs, and school notice boards use pictographs for attendance.

items.text: Key: 1 🍦 = 5 ice creams. 35 ice creams need ___ pictures.
Scale: 1 unit = 10 km. A bar 4 units long shows ___ km.
In a bar graph, all bars should have the same ___.

quiz.q: In a pictograph, 1 🍪 = 10 cookies. Riya's row shows 4 🍪. How many cookies did she bake?
quiz.explain: Each picture means 10 cookies, so 4 pictures mean 4 × 10 = 40.
quiz.mistake: Counts the pictures without using the key (4) or adds 4 + 10

quiz.q: Key: 1 🚂 = 100 passengers. How many 🚂 pictures show 350 passengers?
quiz.explain: 300 passengers need 3 pictures and the extra 50 is half of 100, so half a picture: 3 and a half.
quiz.mistake: Drops the extra 50 (3) or rounds up (4)

quiz.q: A sweet shop sold laddoos in Diwali week: Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40. On which day were the most laddoos sold?
quiz.explain: 40 is the largest value, so Thursday has the longest bar.
steps: So the most laddoos were sold on Thursday.
quiz.mistake: Picks the second-longest bar

quiz.q: Using the same laddoo data (Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40), how many laddoos were sold on Monday and Wednesday together?
quiz.explain: Monday 20 + Wednesday 15 = 35 laddoos.
steps: So 35 laddoos were sold on those two days.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding (5)

quiz.q: Aisha's bar graph uses the scale 1 unit = 5 students. The bar for Kabaddi is 6 units long. How many students chose Kabaddi?
quiz.explain: Each unit stands for 5 students, so 6 units stand for 6 × 5 = 30 students.
quiz.mistake: Reads the bar length without the scale (6) or adds 6 + 5

quiz.q: Four baskets hold 120, 80, 200 and 150 mangoes. Which scale is best for a bar graph in your notebook?
quiz.explain: With 1 unit = 20, the bars are 6, 4, 10 and 7.5 units long: they fit and are easy to draw. 1 mango per unit makes bars far too long; 1000 makes them tiny; 7 gives awkward numbers.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about whether the bars will fit on the page

quiz.q: Key: 1 🌳 = 8 trees. How many trees does half a 🌳 show?
quiz.explain: Half of 8 is 4.
steps: So half a tree picture shows 4 trees.
quiz.mistake: Treats half a picture as a whole picture (8) or doubles it (16)

quiz.q: Joseph's bar graph shows that Class 6A read 32 books and Class 6B read 24 books. How many more books did 6A read?
quiz.explain: 32 − 24 = 8 more books.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two values (56) instead of subtracting

teach.ask: Gappu sees a pictograph of mangoes: 'There are only 3 mango pictures. Does that mean 3 mangoes?'
teach.praise: Chirp! I must read the key first. If 1 picture means 10 mangoes, 3 pictures mean 30!
teach.nudge: Is there something on the graph that tells me what one picture is worth?

revise.summary: A pictograph shows data with pictures, and its key tells what one picture stands for. A bar graph uses bars of the same width with equal gaps, and a scale tells what each unit of length means.
focus: Use the key to read pictographs, including half pictures
Use the scale to read bar lengths
Choose a scale so bars fit on the page
Give every graph a title and axis labels
remember: Value = number of pictures × key (half a picture = half the key value)
Bar graph: same-width bars with equal gaps; bar length shows the value
Value = bar length × scale (6 units × 5 = 30)
traps: Don't count pictures without using the key
Don't read a bar's length without its scale
Half a picture is half the key value, not a whole picture

learn.hook: A pictograph can tell a whole story at a glance, but only if you read the key!
points: Always read the key first: if 1 🍎 = 10 apples, then 3 🍎 = 30 apples.
Maximum and minimum: the row with the most pictures is the largest; the row with the fewest is the smallest.
Find totals by adding rows, and compare by subtracting.
Check claims carefully: 'more than double' means more than 2 times. If A = 40 and B = 25, A is not more than double B, because 2 × 25 = 50 and 40 is less than 50.

example.q: Key: 1 📕 = 5 books. Class 6A has 7 📕 and Class 6B has 3 📕. Did 6A read more than double what 6B read?

learn.reallife: News channels show pictographs of crops, voters and rainfall. Reading the key stops you from being fooled.

games.title: Check the claim
items: If A = 50 and B = 20, A is more than double B.
If A = 30 and B = 20, A is more than double B.
Without the key, you can read exact values.
You need to know what one picture is worth.
The row with the fewest pictures shows the minimum.
If all pictures have the same value.
Half a picture shows half the key value.
That is the rule for part symbols.

quiz.q: Key: 1 🥛 = 10 litres. Dairy A has 6 🥛, Dairy B has 4 🥛 and half a 🥛. How much more milk does A give?
quiz.explain: A = 60 L, B = 45 L, so 60 − 45 = 15 litres.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the half picture

quiz.q: Key: 1 🌳 = 20 trees. Village P has 5 🌳, Q has 2 🌳 and R has 3 🌳. How many trees in all?
quiz.explain: 10 pictures × 20 = 200 trees.
quiz.mistake: Counts pictures instead of trees

quiz.q: Using that pictograph (P 5 🌳, Q 2 🌳, R 3 🌳), which village has the fewest trees and how many?
quiz.explain: Q has the fewest pictures: 2 × 20 = 40 trees.
steps: Key: 1 🌳 = 20 trees. Rows: P 5, Q 2, R 3 pictures.
The fewest pictures is 2, for Q.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of pictures, not trees

quiz.q: Rakesh says: 'Village P has more than double the trees of village Q.' (P = 100, Q = 40.) Is he right?
quiz.explain: Double 40 is 80, and 100 is more than 80.
quiz.mistake: Compares with Q instead of double Q

quiz.q: Key: 1 🎈 = 6 balloons. Asha sold 4 🎈 and Bina sold 2 🎈 and half a 🎈. Is Asha's sale more than double Bina's?
quiz.explain: Asha: 24. Bina: 15. Double 15 is 30, and 24 is less than 30.
quiz.mistake: Compares pictures without working out values

quiz.q: Key: 1 ⚽ = 8 goals. Team X has 3 ⚽ and a quarter ⚽. How many goals?
quiz.explain: 3 × 8 = 24 and a quarter of 8 is 2: 26 goals.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the part picture

quiz.q: A pictograph has no key. What can you say?
options: Only which row has more pictures, not exact values
quiz.explain: Without a key you can compare rows but cannot find actual amounts.
steps: The key tells how many each picture stands for.
Without it, we cannot find exact amounts or the total.
We can still see which row has more pictures.
So only comparisons are possible, not exact values.
Answer: Only which row has more pictures, not exact values
quiz.mistake: Assumes each picture means 1

quiz.q: Key: 1 🍕 = 4 pizzas. Monday shows 9 🍕 and Tuesday 6 🍕. How many pizzas were sold in the two days?
quiz.explain: 15 pictures × 4 = 60 pizzas.
quiz.mistake: Adds pictures but forgets the key

teach.ask: Gappu sees 3 🐛 in a pictograph. 'So there are 3 worms, right?'
teach.praise: Chirp! First read the key. If 1 🐛 = 10 worms, 3 🐛 is 30!
teach.nudge: What does one picture stand for?

revise.summary: To read a pictograph, read the key first, then find values, maximum, minimum, totals and differences. Check claims like 'more than double' by comparing with 2 times the other value.
focus: Convert pictures to values using the key, including part pictures
Find the largest, smallest, totals and differences
Check 'more than double' claims correctly
remember: Read the key first: if 1 🍎 = 10 apples, then 3 🍎 = 30 apples
More than double means more than 2 times
A = 40, B = 25: 2 × 25 = 50, so 40 is not more than double
traps: Don't ignore half or quarter pictures
Compare with double the other value, not the value itself
Without a key you can only say which row has more pictures, not exact values

learn.hook: Turn a boring table into a picture story. Choose your symbol and your key!
points: Choose a symbol and a key. A good key makes most values whole numbers of pictures: if the data are 20, 35, 40, 15, the key 1 picture = 5 works well.
Number of pictures = value ÷ key. 35 ÷ 5 = 7 pictures.
If a value is not a multiple of the key, use part of a symbol: with 1 picture = 10, the value 25 needs 2 and a half pictures.
Values like 23 with a key of 10 are hard to draw (2 and 3 tenths of a picture). That is a drawback of pictographs; pick a better key or round carefully.

example.q: Draw a pictograph for books read: Ali 30, Bela 45, Charu 20. Key: 1 📗 = 10 books.
steps: Write the title, the names, the pictures and the key.

learn.reallife: School notice boards show pictographs of attendance or trees planted using symbols like 🙂 or 🌱.

items.text: Data 10, 25, 40, 15: a good key is 1 picture = ___
Data 100, 300, 250: a good key is 1 picture = ___

quiz.q: Key: 1 🌻 = 5 flowers. How many 🌻 do you draw for 40 flowers?
quiz.explain: 40 ÷ 5 = 8 pictures.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: Key: 1 🚲 = 10 cycles. How should you draw 65 cycles?
quiz.explain: 65 ÷ 10 = 6.5, so 6 whole pictures and half a picture.
steps: 6.5 = 6 whole pictures and half a picture.
quiz.mistake: Rounds instead of using a half symbol

quiz.q: Data: 12, 18, 30, 24. Which key makes every value a whole number of pictures?
quiz.explain: 12, 18, 30 and 24 are all multiples of 6.
steps: Each value must divide exactly by the key.
With 5, 12 ÷ 5 is not whole; with 4, 18 ÷ 4 is not; with 10, 12 ÷ 10 is not.
quiz.mistake: Picks a key that does not divide all values

quiz.q: With the key 1 picture = 10, why is the value 37 hard to show?
options: 37 ÷ 10 is 3.7, which needs 7 tenths of a picture
quiz.explain: Drawing 0.7 of a picture exactly is difficult, so pictographs work best with multiples of the key.
steps: That is 3 whole pictures and 7 tenths of a picture.
7 tenths of a picture is hard to draw exactly.
Answer: 37 ÷ 10 is 3.7, which needs 7 tenths of a picture
quiz.mistake: Does not see the part-picture problem

quiz.q: Rina draws 9 🎫 for 45 tickets. What key did she use?
quiz.explain: 45 ÷ 9 = 5, so each picture is 5 tickets.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of pictures as the key

quiz.q: Key: 1 🐟 = 20 fish. A fisherman caught 150 fish. How many pictures?
quiz.explain: 150 ÷ 20 = 7.5, so 7 whole pictures and half a picture.
steps: So 7 whole pictures and half a picture (7.5).
quiz.mistake: Divides by 10

quiz.q: Which must every pictograph show?
options: A title, the categories and the key
quiz.explain: Readers need the title, labels and key to understand it.
steps: Readers need to know what the pictograph is about → title.
They need to know what each row is → categories.
They need to know what one picture stands for → key.
So a title, the categories and the key.
Answer: A title, the categories and the key
quiz.mistake: Leaves out the key

quiz.q: Data: 200, 350, 500, 150 people. Which key keeps the pictograph short but easy to read?
quiz.explain: With 1 = 50: 4, 7, 10 and 3 pictures, all whole numbers.
steps: All are whole and small numbers.
1 = 1 needs hundreds of pictures; 1 = 7 and 1 = 3 do not divide evenly.
quiz.mistake: Picks a key so small the rows get too long

teach.ask: Gappu wants to draw 60 seeds in a pictograph. 'Must I draw 60 pictures?'
teach.praise: Tweet! With 1 picture = 10 seeds, just 6 pictures do the job!
teach.nudge: Could one picture stand for more than one seed?

revise.summary: To draw a pictograph, choose a symbol and a key that makes most values whole numbers of pictures. Number of pictures = value ÷ key, using part of a symbol when needed.
focus: Find the number of pictures as value ÷ key
Choose a key that divides all the values
Draw half symbols for values that are not multiples of the key
Find the key from the number of pictures
remember: Number of pictures = value ÷ key: 35 ÷ 5 = 7
With 1 picture = 10, the value 25 needs 2 and a half pictures
Every pictograph shows a title, the categories and the key
traps: Divide by the key; don't multiply
Don't round when a half symbol is needed
Don't leave out the key

learn.hook: A bar graph can show a story over time: rising, falling or staying steady!
points: Read the scale first, then each bar's length, to get the values.
Highest bar = largest value; lowest bar = smallest value. Totals: add the values. Comparisons: subtract.
When bars are in time order (hours, days, years), look for a trend: going up, going down, or rising then falling.
Explain the trend with real reasons: traffic is heavy at 9 am and 6 pm because people travel to and from work and school.

example.q: Vehicles passing a crossing (1 unit = 100 vehicles): 7 am 2 units, 9 am 8 units, 12 pm 4 units, 6 pm 9 units. Describe the trend.
steps: Traffic rises in the morning rush, falls at noon and is highest in the evening rush.
example.answer: Two rush hours, peak at 6 pm

learn.reallife: Weather reports show rainfall bars month by month: the monsoon months stand out tall.

games.title: What does the graph say?
items: If bars keep getting taller over the years, the trend is rising.
You can read a bar's value without knowing the scale.
The scale tells what each unit means.
In the vehicle graph, noon is busier than 9 am.
Traffic is high at 9 am because people go to work and school.
That is a sensible reason for the trend.

quiz.q: Using the vehicle data (7 am 200, 9 am 800, 12 pm 400, 6 pm 900), how many vehicles passed in all four hours?
quiz.mistake: Leaves out one bar

quiz.q: How many more vehicles passed at 6 pm than at 12 pm?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two bars

quiz.q: A town's population (1 unit = 1000 people): 2000: 5 units, 2010: 7 units, 2020: 10 units. What is the trend?
quiz.explain: 5000 → 7000 → 10,000: the population keeps growing.
steps: Each value is bigger than the one before.
quiz.mistake: Reads the bars backwards

quiz.q: In that town, by how many people did the population grow from 2000 to 2020?
quiz.explain: 10 − 5 = 5 units, and 5 × 1000 = 5000 people.
quiz.mistake: Gives the answer in units, not people

quiz.q: Rainfall bars for June, July, August and September are much taller than other months. Why?
quiz.explain: Most of India gets its heavy rain in the monsoon.
steps: June to September are the monsoon months in most of India.
Most of the year's heavy rain falls then.
So their bars are much taller.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the graph to a real reason

quiz.q: Ice-cream sales (in cones): Jan 50, Mar 150, May 300, Jul 200. Which month had the highest sales?
quiz.explain: May has the tallest bar: 300 cones.
steps: So May had the highest sales.
quiz.mistake: Picks the last month

quiz.q: Using the ice-cream data, what is a sensible reason May sales are highest?
options: May is the hottest month in many places
quiz.explain: Hot weather makes people buy more ice cream.
steps: May is the hottest month in many places in India.
Hot weather makes people buy more ice cream.
May is not winter and does not have the most days.
So the reason is the heat in May.
Answer: May is the hottest month in many places
quiz.mistake: Gives a reason that does not fit

quiz.q: Using the ice-cream data, May sales were how many times January sales?
steps: So May sales were 6 times January sales.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of dividing

teach.ask: Gappu sees bars growing taller every year in a graph of trees planted. 'What does that tell me?'
teach.praise: Chirp! A rising trend: more trees planted every year!
teach.nudge: Are the bars getting longer or shorter over time?

revise.summary: To read a bar graph, read the scale first, then each bar's length to get the values. When bars are in time order, look for a trend and explain it with real reasons.
focus: Find values, totals and differences from bars using the scale
Describe a trend: going up, going down, or rising then falling
Give a sensible real-life reason for a trend
Compare values by 'how many more' or 'how many times'
remember: Highest bar = largest value; lowest bar = smallest value
Totals: add the values; comparisons: subtract
Traffic is heavy at 9 am and 6 pm because people travel to and from work and school
traps: Don't leave out a bar when adding a total
Give answers in real values (people), not in units
'How many times' means divide, not subtract

learn.hook: Grab a ruler: we're turning a table into a bar graph, step by step!
points: Step 1: Draw two axes (a horizontal line and a vertical line) meeting at a corner.
Step 2: Label one axis with the categories and the other with the values. Give the graph a title.
Step 3: Choose a scale, such as 1 unit = 5 students, and mark 0, 5, 10, 15, ... evenly along the value axis.
Step 4: Bar height = value ÷ scale. 30 students ÷ 5 = 6 units.
Step 5: Draw bars of equal width with equal gaps between them.

example.q: Draw a bar graph: Kabaddi 20, Kho-kho 35, Cricket 45, Chess 10 students. Scale 1 unit = 5 students.
steps: Draw and label the axes, mark 0, 5, 10, ..., 45.
Draw four equal-width bars 4, 7, 9 and 2 units high, with equal gaps.

learn.reallife: Report cards, sports-day results and election results on TV are often shown as bar graphs.

games.title: Planning the bars
games.prompt: Each step needs the one before it
items: Find the largest value in the table
Choose a scale that fits that value on the page
Work out each bar's height (value ÷ scale)
Draw bars of those heights with equal widths and gaps

quiz.q: Scale: 1 unit = 5 students. How tall is the bar for 45 students?
quiz.explain: 45 ÷ 5 = 9 units.
steps: So the bar is 9 units tall.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the scale

quiz.q: Scale: 1 unit = 10 km. How tall is the bar for 75 km?
steps: So the bar is 7.5 units tall.
quiz.mistake: Rounds the bar height

quiz.q: Which is NOT a rule for a good bar graph?
options: Every bar must have a different colour
quiz.explain: Colours are optional; widths, gaps and the scale are what matter.
steps: Rules: equal bar widths, equal gaps, and an evenly marked scale.
Colours are optional; bars may be the same colour.
So 'every bar must have a different colour' is not a rule.
Answer: Every bar must have a different colour
quiz.mistake: Thinks decoration is a rule

quiz.q: A tally table shows Red 10, Blue 15 and Green 5. Using 1 unit = 5, what are the bar heights?
quiz.mistake: Uses the values as heights

quiz.q: Where do the category names (like days of the week) go?
options: Along the axis under or beside the bars
At the top of each bar
quiz.explain: Categories label one axis; values go on the other.
steps: A bar graph has two axes.
One axis shows the categories (days); the other shows the values.
So category names go along the axis under or beside the bars.
Answer: Along the axis under or beside the bars
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two axes

quiz.q: The value axis is marked 0, 5, 10, 15, 25. What is wrong?
options: 20 is missing, so the marks are not evenly spaced
quiz.explain: Marks must go up by the same step: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
steps: The marks go 0, 5, 10, 15 and then jump to 25.
The marks must go up by the same step: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
So the mistake is that the marks are not evenly spaced.
Answer: 20 is missing, so the marks are not evenly spaced
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the uneven scale

quiz.q: Scale: 1 unit = 20 trees. A bar is 6 units tall. How many trees does it show?
quiz.mistake: Divides instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Kiran draws a bar 4 units tall for 60 mangoes. What scale did she use?
quiz.explain: 60 ÷ 4 = 15, so 1 unit = 15 mangoes.
steps: So the scale is 1 unit = 15 mangoes.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 60 by 4

teach.ask: Gappu has the data 10, 25, 40 and a scale of 1 unit = 5. 'How tall is each bar?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Divide each value by 5: bars of 2, 5 and 8 units!
teach.nudge: What should you do with each value and the scale?

revise.summary: To draw a bar graph, draw and label two axes, give a title, choose a scale and mark it evenly, then draw bars of equal width with equal gaps. Bar height = value ÷ scale.
focus: Find bar height as value ÷ scale, including half units
Find a value from a bar (height × scale) and a scale from a bar
Mark the value axis evenly and put categories on the other axis
remember: Bar height = value ÷ scale: 30 students ÷ 5 = 6 units
Bars: equal width, equal gaps
Scale marks must be evenly spaced: 0, 5, 10, 15, ...
traps: To find bar height, divide by the scale; don't multiply
Different colours for each bar are not a rule
Don't skip a mark like 20 on the value axis

topics.title: Fixing bar graphs and finding totals

learn.hook: Oh no, someone spilled ink on the graph! Can you work out what's hidden?
points: Find the scale from a known bar: if the bar for 30 is 6 units tall, then 1 unit = 30 ÷ 6 = 5.
Use that scale to read or redraw erased bars.
Spot mistakes: bars of different widths, uneven gaps, a scale that jumps (0, 10, 20, 40) or a bar of the wrong height.
Totals from a frequency table: multiply each value by its frequency and add. If 5 families have 2 children and 3 have 3 children, that is 5 × 2 + 3 × 3 = 19 children.

example.q: A bar for 24 runs is 8 units tall. Another bar is 5 units tall. How many runs does it show?

learn.reallife: Teachers check graphs in project files, and newspapers correct graphs when readers spot errors.

games.title: Spot the error
items: A bar graph may have bars of different widths.
If 6 units show 30, then 1 unit shows 5.
Total children = sum of (number of children × number of families).
Multiply each value by its frequency.
Gaps between bars should be equal.
That is a rule for bar graphs.

quiz.q: On a graph, the bar for 40 students is 8 units tall. What is the scale?
quiz.explain: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 students per unit.
quiz.mistake: Uses the number of units as the scale

quiz.q: Same graph (1 unit = 5). One bar is erased but the table says 35. How tall should it be?
quiz.explain: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 units.
steps: So the bar should be 7 units tall.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: A graph's scale is 1 unit = 10. The bar for 50 is drawn 4 units tall. What is the mistake?
quiz.explain: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 units, not 4.
steps: So the mistake: it should be 5 units tall.
Answer: It should be 5 units tall
quiz.mistake: Does not check bars against the scale

quiz.q: Children in families: 1 child: 6 families, 2 children: 8 families, 3 children: 2 families. How many children in all?
quiz.mistake: Adds the families (16) instead

quiz.q: Marks in a 5-mark quiz: 3 marks: 4 students, 4 marks: 5 students, 5 marks: 1 student. What is the total of all marks?
steps: So all the marks add up to 37.
quiz.mistake: Adds only the marks 3 + 4 + 5

quiz.q: How many students took that quiz (4 + 5 + 1)?
quiz.explain: 4 + 5 + 1 = 10 students.
steps: 37 is the total of marks, not students.
quiz.mistake: Adds the marks instead of the frequencies

quiz.q: In a bar graph the gaps between bars are 1 cm, 1 cm and 3 cm. What should be fixed?
quiz.explain: Bar graphs need equal gaps between bars.
steps: Gaps are 1 cm, 1 cm and 3 cm — not the same.
A bar graph needs equal gaps between bars.
Bars in a bar graph should not touch.
So the gaps must be made equal.
Answer: The gaps must be equal
quiz.mistake: Thinks gap size does not matter

quiz.q: A bar for 18 is 6 units tall. The bar for Sunday is 9 units tall. What does Sunday show?
quiz.explain: Scale: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 per unit. 9 × 3 = 27.
quiz.mistake: Adds 9 + 18

teach.ask: Gappu found a graph where 10 worms is a bar 2 units tall. 'How tall is the bar for 25 worms?'
teach.praise: Chirp! 1 unit = 5 worms, so 25 worms is 5 units tall!
teach.nudge: What does one unit stand for in this graph?

revise.summary: Find a graph's scale from a known bar, then use it to read or redraw bars and spot mistakes. Totals from a frequency table are found by multiplying each value by its frequency and adding.
focus: Find the scale as value ÷ bar height
Spot mistakes: unequal widths or gaps, a jumping scale, wrong bar heights
Find totals from a frequency table using value × frequency
remember: Bar for 30 is 6 units → 1 unit = 30 ÷ 6 = 5
5 families with 2 children and 3 with 3: 5 × 2 + 3 × 3 = 19 children
traps: Don't use the number of units as the scale
Don't add only the frequencies when the total of values is asked
Gaps between bars must be equal

topics.title: Column graphs, horizontal bars and infographics

learn.hook: A graph can be honest or it can trick you. Learn to spot the difference!
points: Vertical bars (a column graph) suit things that go up, like heights of buildings or trees.
Horizontal bars suit things that go across, like lengths of rivers or distances between cities.
An infographic decorates a graph with pictures to make the data attractive and easy to understand.
Fancy pictures can distort data: a picture made twice as tall AND twice as wide looks 4 times bigger, even though the value only doubled.
Pictographs and bar graphs give quick comparisons, but they must always state their scale.

example.q: Should the lengths of four Indian rivers be shown with vertical or horizontal bars?
steps: Rivers are long things that stretch across.
Horizontal bars match the idea of length.
Use horizontal bars with a scale like 1 unit = 200 km.

learn.reallife: Newspapers use infographics for budget, cricket and election data. A good reader always checks the scale.

games.title: Honest graphs
items: Doubling both width and height of a picture makes it look 4 times as big.
An infographic must never use pictures.
Pictures are what make it an infographic.
Every bar graph should state its scale.
A graph that starts its scale at 90 instead of 0 can make small differences look huge.
They work just like vertical bars.

quiz.q: Which data suits a vertical (column) graph best?
quiz.explain: Heights go upwards, so vertical bars match them.
steps: Heights go upwards too, so they match vertical bars.
River lengths, distances and road lengths stretch across.
quiz.mistake: Picks a length that runs across

quiz.q: Which data suits horizontal bars best?
options: Lengths of rivers like the Ganga and Godavari
quiz.explain: Lengths stretch across, so horizontal bars fit.
steps: Horizontal bars stretch across the page.
Lengths of rivers stretch across too.
Heights of trees, students and towers go upwards (vertical bars).
Answer: Lengths of rivers like the Ganga and Godavari
quiz.mistake: Mixes up height and length data

quiz.q: An infographic shows one bag of rice for 100 kg and a bag twice as tall and twice as wide for 200 kg. What is the problem?
options: The bags are the wrong colour
The bigger bag looks 4 times bigger, though the value only doubled
quiz.explain: Area grows 2 × 2 = 4 times, which exaggerates the difference.
steps: The value only doubles: 100 kg → 200 kg.
But the bag is twice as tall AND twice as wide.
Its area grows 2 × 2 = 4 times, so it looks 4 times bigger.
Answer: The bigger bag looks 4 times bigger, though the value only doubled
quiz.mistake: Thinks a bigger picture is always fair

quiz.q: What is an infographic?
options: A graph decorated with pictures to share data attractively
quiz.explain: Infographics combine data with pictures and design.
steps: An infographic shows data with pictures and design.
It aims to share data in an attractive way.
It is not a wrong graph, a number list or a tally mark.
Answer: A graph decorated with pictures to share data attractively
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is just a picture without data

quiz.q: A graph shows scores 92 and 96, but its value axis starts at 90. The second bar looks 3 times as tall. Is that fair?
options: No, the real difference is only 4 marks
quiz.explain: Starting at 90 makes 2 vs 6 units, which hides that the scores are close.
steps: Scores 92 and 96 differ by only 96 − 92 = 4 marks.
Starting the axis at 90 makes the bars 2 and 6 units tall.
6 ÷ 2 = 3, so one looks 3 times as tall, which is misleading.
Answer: No, the real difference is only 4 marks
quiz.mistake: Trusts bar size without reading the scale

quiz.q: Rivers: A 2500 km, B 1500 km, C 1000 km. With horizontal bars and 1 unit = 500 km, how long is bar A?
steps: So bar A is 5 units long.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 1000

quiz.q: With 1 unit = 500 km, how many units longer is river A's bar than river C's?
quiz.explain: A: 5 units, C: 2 units. 5 − 2 = 3 units.
steps: So A's bar is 3 units longer.
quiz.mistake: Gives the difference in km

quiz.q: What must every pictograph and bar graph state so it can be read correctly?
quiz.explain: Without the scale, we can't know what a bar or symbol stands for.
steps: To read values from a graph we must know what one symbol or unit stands for.
That is the scale or key.
Colour, artist and date do not help read values.
So every graph must state its scale (key).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the scale

teach.ask: Gappu sees a graph where one tree picture is huge and the other small. 'Does the big tree have many more?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Check the scale first. A big picture can trick your eyes!
teach.nudge: What should you read before trusting the size of a picture?

revise.summary: Vertical bars (column graphs) suit things that go up, and horizontal bars suit things that go across. Infographics decorate data with pictures, but fancy pictures or cut axes can distort the data.
focus: Choose vertical or horizontal bars for the data
Know what an infographic is
Spot pictures or scales that make data look misleading
remember: Vertical bars: heights (buildings, trees); horizontal bars: lengths (rivers, distances)
Infographic: a graph decorated with pictures to make data attractive and easy to understand
A picture twice as tall AND twice as wide looks 4 times bigger
traps: A bigger picture is not always fair: doubling the value does not mean doubling both height and width
Don't trust bar size without reading the scale
Every pictograph and bar graph must state its scale (key)
